chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Work, energy and power are fundamental concepts in physics.
All living beings and machines need energy to perform activities.
The Sun is the biggest natural source of energy for us.
Energy exists in many forms: kinetic, potential, heat, chemical, electrical and light energy.
The unit of both work and energy is joule (J). The unit of power is watt (W).
The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

10.1.3 Work Done by a Constant Force

DEFINITION: Work is said to be done when a force acts on an object and the object is displaced in the direction of the applied force. Work done = Force x Displacement (W = F x s). The SI unit of work is joule (J). 1 joule = 1 newton x 1 metre.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: For work to be done, two conditions must be satisfied: (i) a force should act on the object, and (ii) the object must be displaced.
If either condition is not met, work is not done in the scientific sense.
Work has only magnitude and no direction (it is a scalar quantity).
Work done is positive when force and displacement are in the same direction.
Work done is negative when force and displacement are in opposite directions.
Work done is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement or when displacement is zero.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.1:
sections.aim: To identify situations where work is done in the scientific sense.
procedure: For each activity from daily life, ask: (i) What is the work being done on? (ii) What is happening to the object? (iii) Who (or what) is doing the work?
sections.observation: Activities like pushing a rock that does not move, or standing still with a heavy load, do not involve scientific work despite physical effort.
sections.conclusion: Work in science requires both a force and a displacement of the object on which the force acts.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.2:
sections.aim: To think of daily-life situations involving work.
procedure: Think of situations from daily life involving work, list them, discuss whether work is done, identify the force and the object, and determine what happens to the object.
sections.observation: A bullock pulling a cart, a girl pulling a trolley, lifting a book - all involve force and displacement, hence work is done.
sections.conclusion: Work is done whenever force causes displacement in an object.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.3:
sections.aim: To identify situations where object is not displaced despite a force, and situations where object gets displaced in the absence of a force.
procedure: Think of situations where: (a) object is not displaced despite a force (e.g., pushing a wall), (b) object is displaced in the absence of apparent force (e.g., a ball rolling on a smooth surface).
sections.observation: When there is no displacement, no work is done even if force is applied. When displacement occurs without an apparent external force, the object was already in motion.
sections.conclusion: Only when force produces displacement is work said to be done.

sections.label: EXERCISE 10.1:
sections.raw:
Q: A force of 7 N acts on an object. The displacement is 8 m in the direction of the force. Let the force act on the object through the displacement. What is the work done in this case?
A: W = F x s = 7 N x 8 m = 56 J. The work done is 56 J.

items.question: When do we say that work is done?
items.answer:
Work is done when:
(i) A force acts on an object.
(ii) The object is displaced in the direction of the applied force.
Both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for work to be done.

items.question: Write the SI unit of work and define it.
items.answer:
The SI unit of work is joule (J).
Definition: 1 joule is the amount of work done when a force of 1 newton displaces an object through 1 metre in the direction of the force.
1 J = 1 N x 1 m = 1 N m.

items.question: What is the formula for work done by a constant force?
items.answer:
Work done = Force x Displacement
W = F x s
Where W = work done (in joules), F = force applied (in newtons), s = displacement (in metres) in the direction of the force.

items.question: When is work done said to be negative?
items.answer:
Work done is said to be negative when the force acts in the direction opposite to the displacement. In this case, the work done by the force is denoted by a minus sign: W = F x (-s) or W = -F x s.
Example: A retarding force applied to stop a moving ball does negative work.

items.question: A force of 5 N acts on an object displaced through 2 m in the direction of the force. What is the work done?
items.answer:
W = F x s
W = 5 N x 2 m
W = 10 N m = 10 J
The work done is 10 joules.

items.question: A pair of bullocks exerts a force of 140 N on a plough. The field being ploughed is 15 m long. How much work is done in ploughing the length of the field?
items.answer:
W = F x s
W = 140 N x 15 m
W = 2100 N m = 2100 J
The work done in ploughing the field is 2100 J.

items.question: Explain with an example why a person pushing a wall does no work in the scientific sense even though they get tired.
items.answer:
For work to be done in the scientific sense, two conditions must be met:
(i) A force must act on the object.
(ii) The object must get displaced.
When a person pushes a wall:
- A force is applied on the wall. Condition (i) is satisfied.
- The wall does not move. There is zero displacement. Condition (ii) is NOT satisfied.
Since displacement is zero: W = F x 0 = 0
Therefore, no work is done on the wall.
The person gets tired because internal muscular energy is used, but no mechanical work is done on the wall.

items.question: Distinguish between positive work and negative work with one example each.
items.answer:
POSITIVE WORK:
- When force and displacement are in the same direction.
- Example: A boy pushing a cart forward - the cart moves in the direction of the applied force. Work done is positive.
- W = +F x s

NEGATIVE WORK:
- When force and displacement are in opposite directions.
- Example: A ball thrown upward - gravity acts downward while the ball moves upward. Work done by gravity is negative.
- W = -F x s

In both cases, the magnitude of work = force x displacement, but the sign indicates direction of energy transfer.

items.question: Is work done by gravity when a ball thrown upward rises to its maximum height? Justify.
items.answer:
Yes, work is done by gravity, and it is negative.
- The ball thrown upward moves upward (displacement is upward).
- Gravity always acts downward.
- Force (downward) is opposite to displacement (upward).
Therefore, work done by gravity = -F x s = -mgs (where s is height reached).
This negative work means gravity is taking away energy from the ball, which is why the ball slows down as it rises.
At maximum height, velocity = 0 and all kinetic energy has been converted to potential energy.

items.question: A porter lifts a luggage of 15 kg from the ground and puts it on his head 1.5 m above the ground. Calculate the work done by him on the luggage.
items.answer:
Given:
Mass of luggage, m = 15 kg
Displacement, s = 1.5 m
Acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m/s^2

Force applied = weight of luggage = m x g = 15 x 10 = 150 N

Work done, W = F x s = mg x s
W = 15 kg x 10 m/s^2 x 1.5 m
W = 225 kg m/s^2 x m
W = 225 N m = 225 J

The work done by the porter on the luggage is 225 J.

items.question: What is work done when force is zero? What is work done when displacement is zero? Explain with suitable situations.
items.answer:
CASE 1 - Force is zero:
W = F x s = 0 x s = 0
Work done is zero.
Situation: A ball rolling on a perfectly smooth, frictionless horizontal surface continues to move without any force. No work is done on it.

CASE 2 - Displacement is zero:
W = F x s = F x 0 = 0
Work done is zero.
Situation: A person holds a heavy book standing still. Even though force (weight of book) acts, there is no displacement, so no work is done on the book.

In both cases, the mathematical product W = F x s = 0. Work is done only when both force and displacement are non-zero and have a component along each other.

items.question: The SI unit of work is:
items.explanation: Work = Force x Displacement. SI unit = N x m = joule (J). Newton is unit of force, watt is unit of power, pascal is unit of pressure.

items.question: Work is done when:

options.A: force is applied but no displacement occurs
options.B: force is applied and displacement occurs in direction of force

items.explanation: For work to be done, both force and displacement must exist and displacement should be in (or have a component in) the direction of force. If displacement is zero or perpendicular, work done is zero.

items.question: A force of 10 N displaces an object by 5 m in the direction of the force. Work done is:
items.explanation: W = F x s = 10 N x 5 m = 50 J. Simply multiply force by displacement in the direction of force.

items.question: When a ball is thrown upward, the work done by gravity is:
items.explanation: Gravity acts downward, but displacement of ball is upward. Force and displacement are in opposite directions, so work done by gravity = -mgs, which is negative.

items.question: 1 joule is defined as work done when a force of 1 N displaces an object through:
items.explanation: 1 J = 1 N x 1 m. The joule is defined with metre (SI unit of length) and newton (SI unit of force).

items.question: A person holds a 20 kg box stationary on his head for 5 minutes. Work done on the box is:
items.explanation: Although the person exerts force (weight = 200 N upward), displacement of the box is zero. W = F x 0 = 0. No scientific work is done on the box, though the person expends muscular energy.

items.question: A force of F acts in the opposite direction to displacement s. The work done is:
items.explanation: When force and displacement are in opposite directions, work done is negative. W = -Fs. This represents energy being taken away from the object (like friction stopping a moving object).

items.question: A bullock cart is pulled by a force of 200 N. If the work done is 2000 J, the displacement of the cart is:
items.explanation: W = F x s, so s = W/F = 2000/200 = 10 m. Always check: W = 200 x 10 = 2000 J.

items.question: Which of the following involves zero work done in the scientific sense?

options.A: A coolie carrying luggage and walking horizontally
options.B: A ball rolling on ground due to applied force
options.D: A car accelerating due to engine force

items.explanation: A coolie carrying luggage walks horizontally. The force he applies is vertical (upward, to support luggage), but displacement is horizontal. Force is perpendicular to displacement, so work done by the coolie on luggage = 0. Options B, C, D all have force and displacement in the same direction.

items.question: kJ stands for kilojoule. How many joules equal 1 kJ?
items.explanation: The prefix 'kilo' means 1000. So 1 kJ = 1000 J. This is used when dealing with large amounts of energy like food energy.

items.question: An object is moved from point A to point B and back to A by the same path. The total work done by a constant horizontal force F acting in the direction A to B is:

options.A: 2 x F x d (where d = distance AB)

items.explanation: From A to B: displacement = +d, force = +F, work = +Fd. From B to A: displacement = -d (opposite direction), force = +F (unchanged), work = -Fd. Total = Fd + (-Fd) = 0. But wait - this is work done BY the force. Actually, on return journey, force F still acts from A to B direction, but displacement is from B to A. So work on return = F x (-d) = -Fd. Total = Fd + (-Fd) = 0. Net displacement is zero, so net work is zero. Answer (C) 0 is correct.

items.question: Work done by a force on a stationary object is zero. Which of the following CORRECTLY explains why a person standing with heavy luggage gets tired even though no work is done?

options.A: The person does work against gravity
options.B: Internal muscular energy is consumed to maintain the static position
options.C: Potential energy increases in the luggage
options.D: Kinetic energy of the person increases

items.explanation: In the scientific sense, no work is done on the luggage (zero displacement). However, to maintain a static position against gravity, the muscles undergo repeated contractions and relaxations at the cellular level, consuming chemical energy (from food). This internal energy expenditure causes tiredness even though no mechanical work is done on the luggage. Options A and C are incorrect as no work or energy change occurs in the luggage.

subtopics.subtopic_name: NOT MUCH WORK IN SPITE OF WORKING HARD

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Common usage of 'work' includes reading, writing, thinking, exercising etc.
Scientific definition of work is much more specific and limited.
Kamali studying for examinations is a good example: she reads, writes, draws diagrams, attends classes - all considered hard work in common parlance.
But in science, if there is no displacement of an object by a force, this 'hard work' involves very little scientific work.
Pushing a huge rock that does not move = no scientific work done even if person is exhausted.
Standing still with heavy load = no scientific work done on the load.

items.question: Give two examples from daily life where common usage of 'work' differs from the scientific definition of work.
items.answer:
Example 1: Pushing a heavy wall.
- Common sense: Person is working hard.
- Scientific sense: No work done (wall does not move, displacement = 0).

Example 2: A student studying all night.
- Common sense: The student is working very hard.
- Scientific sense: Very little scientific work done (reading and thinking involve no significant displacement of objects by force).

items.question: Explain why climbing a flight of stairs involves scientific work but standing still with a heavy load on your head does not.
items.answer:
CLIMBING STAIRS:
- Force applied: upward (to lift body weight against gravity).
- Displacement: upward (body moves up each step).
- Force and displacement are in the same direction.
- W = F x s = mgs (not zero).
- Scientific work IS done.

STANDING STILL WITH LOAD:
- Force applied: upward (to support the weight of load).
- Displacement: zero (neither person nor load moves vertically).
- W = F x 0 = 0.
- Scientific work is NOT done on the load.

The key difference is displacement. Climbing produces upward displacement, while standing produces none.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: In which of the following is scientific work done?

options.B: A person pushing a wall that does not move
options.C: A coolie lifting a bag from the ground
options.D: A man standing with luggage on his head

items.explanation: Lifting a bag involves force (upward) and displacement (upward), so work is done. Reading involves no physical displacement. Pushing an immovable wall has zero displacement. Standing still has zero displacement.

items.question: A student says she worked hard all day studying. In science, she:

options.B: did no work at all in any sense
options.D: did the same work as a weightlifter

items.explanation: In daily life, studying is considered hard work. In science, work requires force and displacement. Mental activities involve negligible physical force and displacement, so very little scientific work is done.

items.question: Why does a person holding a 10 kg bag stationary at arm's length get tired even though no scientific work is done on the bag?

options.B: Muscular cells continuously contract using chemical energy
options.C: Kinetic energy of the arm increases

items.explanation: Though displacement = 0 means no mechanical work is done, muscles continuously contract and relax at the cellular level to maintain position, consuming chemical (food) energy and causing fatigue.

items.question: Which of the following is an example of zero scientific work?

options.A: A ball rolling down a slope under gravity
options.C: A man carrying a bucket of water while walking horizontally

items.explanation: The force the man applies is vertical (upward, to carry the bucket) but displacement is horizontal. Force is perpendicular to displacement, so work done on the bucket = 0. All other options involve force and displacement in the same direction.

items.question: Ramu pushed a heavy rock with all his strength for 1 hour but it did not move. Somu lifted a 1 kg stone by 1 m. Who did more scientific work?

options.A: Ramu, because he applied more force

items.explanation: Ramu applied force but displacement = 0, so W_Ramu = F x 0 = 0. Somu lifted a stone: W_Somu = mgs = 1 x 10 x 1 = 10 J. Somu did more scientific work despite applying much less force, because displacement occurred. Force alone does not determine work.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Pebble pushed on surface: force acts, pebble moves = work done.
Girl pulls trolley and it moves = work done.
Lifting a book: force applied, book rises = work done.
Key principle: force AND displacement, both must be present.
Work done can be positive, negative or zero.
If force is in direction of displacement: positive work.
If force is opposite to displacement: negative work.
If force is perpendicular to displacement: zero work.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.2:
sections.aim: To understand the scientific conception of work through daily-life examples.
procedure: - Think of daily life situations involving work.
- For each, identify: what is the force acting on? What is happening to the object? Who is doing the work?
- Determine if both conditions (force + displacement) are satisfied.
sections.observation: Only those activities where force produces displacement involve scientific work. Pushing an immovable object, or holding an object stationary, do not constitute work.
sections.conclusion: Work = Force x Displacement (only when force produces displacement of the object on which it acts).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.3:
sections.aim: To identify situations where object is not displaced despite force, and vice versa.
procedure: Think of and list: (a) situations where object is not displaced despite force, (b) situations where object is displaced without apparent force, (c) discuss whether work is done.
sections.observation: A ball rolling on smooth floor moves with no additional force - no work being done on it. A person pushing a wall - no displacement - no work done.

items.question: State the two conditions necessary for work to be done in science.
items.answer:
For work to be done in science, the following two conditions must be satisfied:
(i) A force must act on the object.
(ii) The object must be displaced (moved) by the action of the force.
If either condition is absent, scientific work is zero.

items.question: Give one example each of positive work and negative work. Explain.
items.answer:
POSITIVE WORK: A football player kicks a ball. The force (kick) and the resulting displacement of the ball are in the same direction (forward). W = +Fs. Energy is transferred to the ball, increasing its kinetic energy.

NEGATIVE WORK: A braking force is applied to stop a moving car. The car moves forward (displacement is forward) but the braking force acts backward (opposite direction). W = -Fs. Energy is removed from the car, reducing its kinetic energy and bringing it to rest.

items.question: A girl pulls a trolley through 10 m using a force of 30 N. A boy tries to push a heavy box but it does not move. Compare the work done in both cases and explain.
items.answer:
GIRL PULLING TROLLEY:
- Force = 30 N (in direction of motion)
- Displacement = 10 m
- W = F x s = 30 x 10 = 300 J
- Both conditions satisfied: force is applied AND trolley is displaced.
- Work done = 300 J (positive work).

BOY PUSHING BOX:
- Force = some F N (applied to box)
- Displacement = 0 (box does not move)
- W = F x 0 = 0 J
- Only one condition satisfied: force is applied BUT there is no displacement.
- Work done = 0 J (zero work).

Comparison: The girl does 300 J of work. The boy does 0 J of scientific work despite possibly applying a large force. This shows that force alone, without displacement, does not constitute work.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Work done = 0 when:

options.A: force is large and displacement is small
options.B: force acts but displacement is zero
options.C: displacement is large and force is small
options.D: force and displacement are in same direction

items.explanation: W = F x s. If s = 0, then W = F x 0 = 0, regardless of how large F is. Only when displacement occurs is work done.

items.question: A pebble is pushed on a table and slides 0.5 m under a 2 N force. Work done is:
items.explanation: W = F x s = 2 N x 0.5 m = 1 J. Force and displacement are in same direction, so work is positive.

items.question: A ball is thrown upward. Which force does NEGATIVE work on the ball while it rises?
items.explanation: Both gravity (acts downward, ball moves upward) and air resistance (acts downward, opposing motion, ball moves upward) act opposite to displacement. Both do negative work on the rising ball.

items.question: Which of the following best represents the scientific conception of work?

options.A: Effort or exertion involved in any activity
options.B: Product of force and displacement in the direction of force
options.D: Time taken to complete a task

items.explanation: Scientifically, W = F x s where s is displacement in the direction of force. It is not about effort, energy spent without displacement, or time.

items.question: A satellite orbits Earth in a circular orbit at constant speed. The gravitational force always points toward Earth's center (perpendicular to satellite's motion). Work done by gravity on the satellite per complete orbit is:

options.B: 2 x pi x r x F_gravity

items.explanation: In circular motion, force (gravity) is always perpendicular to displacement (tangential velocity direction). When force is perpendicular to displacement, work done = 0. Over a complete orbit, net displacement is also zero, confirming zero net work by gravity on a satellite in circular orbit.

subtopics.subtopic_name: WORK DONE BY A CONSTANT FORCE

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Work done = Force x Displacement: W = Fs
Unit: newton metre (N m) = joule (J)
Work is a scalar quantity (no direction).
1 joule = work done by 1 N force producing 1 m displacement.
When force acts in the direction of displacement: W = +Fs (positive work).
When force acts opposite to displacement: W = -Fs (negative work), e.g., a retarding force F applied in opposite direction.
Work done can be expressed as W = F x (-s) = -Fs when retarding force opposes displacement.
kJ (kilojoule) = 1000 J (for large energy quantities).
EXAMPLE 10.1:
A force of 5 N acts on an object. The object is displaced through 2 m in the direction of the force. If the force acts on the object all through the displacement, find the work done.
Solution:
F = 5 N, s = 2 m
W = F x s = 5 x 2 = 10 N m = 10 J
Work done is 10 J.
EXAMPLE (from textbook, activity context):
A force of 7 N acts on an object. Displacement = 8 m in direction of force.
W = F x s = 7 x 8 = 56 J.

items.question: Write the formula for work done by a constant force and state the meaning of each symbol.
items.answer:
Formula: W = F x s
Where:
W = Work done (in joules, J)
F = Constant force applied (in newtons, N)
s = Displacement of the object in the direction of force (in metres, m)
The unit of work is N m = joule (J).

items.question: Explain with an example why work done can be negative. Also explain when work done is zero.
items.answer:
NEGATIVE WORK: Work is negative when force and displacement are in opposite directions.
Example: A moving car is braked. The car moves forward (displacement = +s) but braking force acts backward (-F). Work done by braking force = (-F)(s) = -Fs. The negative value shows energy is removed from the car.

ZERO WORK: Work is zero when:
(a) Displacement is zero (e.g., pushing a wall): W = F x 0 = 0.
(b) Force is perpendicular to displacement (e.g., a satellite in circular orbit): force toward center, motion is tangential - perpendicular - so W = 0.

items.question: A force of 5 N acts on an object displaced through 2 m. (i) If force is in direction of displacement, find work done. (ii) If force is opposite to displacement, find work done. What do the signs tell us?
items.answer:
(i) Force in direction of displacement:
W = +F x s = +5 x 2 = +10 J
Positive work: Force transfers energy to the object, increasing its kinetic energy.

(ii) Force opposite to displacement:
W = -F x s = -5 x 2 = -10 J
Negative work: Force takes away energy from the object, decreasing its kinetic energy (like a braking/retarding force).

INTERPRETATION OF SIGNS:
- Positive (+): Energy is given TO the object by the force. Object speeds up.
- Negative (-): Energy is taken FROM the object by the force. Object slows down.
- Zero (0): No energy transfer between force and object.
The sign of work indicates the direction of energy transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: The formula W = F x s gives work done when:

options.B: force is in the direction of displacement
options.C: force acts but object is stationary

items.explanation: W = Fs is valid when force F is in the direction of displacement s. If perpendicular, work = 0. If opposite, work = -Fs.

items.question: If F = 10 N and s = 3 m in the direction of force, work done is:
items.explanation: W = F x s = 10 x 3 = 30 J. Simple multiplication of force and displacement.

items.question: A retarding force of 8 N acts on a moving object and brings it to rest after 4 m. The work done by the retarding force is:
items.explanation: Retarding force acts opposite to direction of motion (displacement). So W = -F x s = -8 x 4 = -32 J. Negative sign shows the force removed kinetic energy from the object.

items.question: 1 kilojoule (kJ) equals:
items.explanation: The prefix 'kilo' means 10^3 = 1000. So 1 kJ = 1000 J. Kilojoules are used when measuring larger energies like food calories or electrical energy.

items.question: An object is displaced by s = 5 m under force F = 6 N (in direction of displacement) and then by s = 3 m under retarding force F = 6 N (opposite to displacement). Total work done is:
items.explanation: Work in first part = +6 x 5 = +30 J. Work in second part = -6 x 3 = -18 J. Total work = 30 + (-18) = 12 J. Work is a scalar and can be added algebraically with sign.

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 10.2.4 Potential Energy of an Object at a Height

DEFINITION: Energy is the capacity of an object to do work. An object that possesses energy can exert a force on another object. When this happens, energy is transferred from the first object to the second. The unit of energy is the same as that of work - joule (J). 1 J is the energy required to do 1 joule of work.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Energy is possessed by an object by virtue of its motion (kinetic energy) or position/configuration (potential energy).
The SI unit of energy is joule (J). 1 kJ = 1000 J.
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed - it can only be transformed from one form to another (Law of Conservation of Energy).
The Sun is the biggest natural source of energy.
Sources of energy: Sun, nuclei of atoms, interior of earth, tides.
An object having capability to do work is said to possess energy.
The object which does work loses energy; the object on which work is done gains energy.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.5:
sections.aim: To list and discuss various sources of energy.
procedure: A few sources of energy are given. List many more sources. Discuss in small groups how certain sources are due to the Sun. Identify sources not due to the Sun.
sections.observation: Most energy sources (wind, water, food, fossil fuels, plants) ultimately derive from solar energy. Tidal energy, geothermal energy and nuclear energy are not solar in origin.
sections.conclusion:
Energy exists in many forms and comes from various natural sources, with the Sun being the primary source for most.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Define energy. What is its SI unit?
items.answer:
Energy is the capacity of an object to do work. An object that possesses energy can exert a force on another object and when it does so, energy is transferred from the first to the second object.
SI unit of energy is joule (J), same as that of work.
1 J = 1 N m. For larger quantities, kilojoule (kJ) is used: 1 kJ = 1000 J.

items.question: Name any four forms of energy.
items.answer:
The four forms of energy are:
(i) Kinetic energy - energy due to motion.
(ii) Potential energy - energy due to position or configuration.
(iii) Heat energy - energy associated with temperature.
(iv) Chemical energy - energy stored in chemical bonds (e.g., food, fuels).
Other forms include electrical energy and light energy.

items.question: State the Law of Conservation of Energy.
items.answer: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy can only be converted from one form to another; it can neither be created nor destroyed. The total energy before and after any transformation always remains the same. This law is valid in all situations and for all kinds of energy transformations.

items.question: Write the formula for kinetic energy of an object. Define each term.
items.answer:
Kinetic energy, E_k = (1/2) m v^2
Where:
m = mass of the object (in kg)
v = velocity of the object (in m/s)
E_k = kinetic energy (in joules, J)
Kinetic energy is always positive (as m and v^2 are always positive).

items.question: Write the formula for gravitational potential energy of an object at a height. Define each term.
items.answer:
Gravitational Potential Energy, E_p = m g h
Where:
m = mass of the object (in kg)
g = acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s^2, approx. 10 m/s^2)
h = height above the ground/reference level (in m)
E_p = potential energy (in joules, J)
It represents the work done against gravity in lifting the object to height h.

items.question: What is the relationship between work done and kinetic energy?
items.answer:
The work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy. This is called the work-energy theorem.
W = Change in KE = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2 = (1/2)m(v^2 - u^2)
Where u = initial velocity and v = final velocity.
If u = 0: W = (1/2)mv^2 = E_k.
The work done on a body from rest equals its final kinetic energy.

items.question: Explain the energy transformation when a fast-moving cricket ball hits a stationary wicket and knocks it away.
items.answer:
INITIAL STATE:
- Cricket ball: moving fast, possesses kinetic energy = (1/2)mv^2.
- Wicket: stationary, kinetic energy = 0.

DURING IMPACT:
- Ball exerts force on wicket.
- Work is done by ball on wicket.
- Energy is transferred from ball to wicket.

FINAL STATE:
- Wicket: moves (thrown away), gains kinetic energy.
- Ball: slows down, loses kinetic energy.

TRANSFORMATION: Kinetic energy of ball is transferred to the wicket as kinetic energy (and some heat/sound due to impact). Total energy remains conserved. This demonstrates both energy transfer during work and the law of conservation of energy.

items.question: Explain what happens to the energy of a freely falling object as it falls from height h to the ground.
items.answer:
Consider an object of mass m falling freely from height h.

AT HEIGHT h (just before release):
- KE = 0 (velocity = 0)
- PE = mgh
- Total mechanical energy = mgh

AT HEIGHT h/2 (midway):
- The object has fallen h/2, velocity v^2 = 2g(h/2) = gh
- KE = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2)m(gh) = mgh/2
- PE = mg(h/2) = mgh/2
- Total = mgh/2 + mgh/2 = mgh (SAME)

AT GROUND (h = 0):
- PE = 0
- KE = (1/2)mv^2, and v^2 = 2gh, so KE = mgh
- Total = mgh (SAME)

CONCLUSION: At every point during free fall, the sum of KE and PE = mgh = constant. PE converts to KE as the object falls. Total mechanical energy is conserved throughout.

items.question: Why does the work done by gravity depend only on vertical height and not on the path taken?
items.answer:
The work done by gravity depends only on vertical height because gravity is a conservative force.

Consider an object moved from A to B via two different paths:
- Path 1: Straight vertical rise of height h.
- Path 2: Inclined or curved path to the same height h.

In both cases, work done by gravity = -mgh (same).
This is because gravity acts only in the vertical direction.
The horizontal component of any displacement involves no work against gravity.

Formula: W_gravity = -mgh (negative because gravity acts downward, displacement is upward).

This height-dependence-only (path-independence) is a key property of gravitational potential energy. The potential energy stored in an object at height h is always mgh, regardless of how it got there.

items.question: An object of mass 15 kg is moving with a uniform velocity of 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
items.answer:
Given:
Mass of object, m = 15 kg
Velocity, v = 4 m/s

Kinetic energy, E_k = (1/2) m v^2
E_k = (1/2) x 15 kg x (4 m/s)^2
E_k = (1/2) x 15 x 16
E_k = (1/2) x 240
E_k = 120 J

The kinetic energy of the object is 120 J.

items.question: Find the energy possessed by an object of mass 10 kg when it is at a height of 6 m above the ground. (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given:
Mass of object, m = 10 kg
Height above ground, h = 6 m
g = 9.8 m/s^2

Gravitational Potential Energy, E_p = mgh
E_p = 10 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 x 6 m
E_p = 10 x 9.8 x 6
E_p = 588 J

The potential energy possessed by the object is 588 J.
(This is also the work done against gravity to lift the object to that height.)

items.question: Two objects of masses 4 kg and 16 kg are moving with the same kinetic energy. The ratio of their velocities (v_4/v_16) is:

items.question: An object of mass 12 kg is at a certain height. Its potential energy is 480 J (g = 10 m/s^2). Find the height.
items.explanation: E_p = mgh. So h = E_p/(mg) = 480/(12 x 10) = 480/120 = 4 m. Always check: 12 x 10 x 4 = 480 J. Correct.

items.question: An object of mass m is dropped from height h. At height h/3 from the ground, what is the ratio of PE to KE?
items.explanation: At height h/3 from ground: PE = mg(h/3). Total energy = mgh. KE = mgh - mg(h/3) = mgh(1 - 1/3) = 2mgh/3. Ratio PE:KE = (mgh/3):(2mgh/3) = 1:2.

items.question: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is thrown upward with initial velocity 20 m/s. At the highest point, its energy is: (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.explanation: Initial KE = (1/2)(0.5)(20)^2 = (1/2)(0.5)(400) = 100 J. At highest point, v = 0, so KE = 0. By conservation of energy, all KE has converted to PE = 100 J. Maximum height h = u^2/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m. PE = mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 20 = 100 J. Total energy = 100 J throughout.

items.question: List any four forms in which energy exists in nature.
items.answer:
Energy exists in nature in the following forms:
(i) Kinetic energy - energy possessed by objects in motion (e.g., moving car, flowing river).
(ii) Potential energy - energy possessed by objects due to their position or configuration (e.g., water in a reservoir, a stretched spring).

items.question: What is mechanical energy? Give examples to show it can be kinetic, potential, or both.
items.answer:
MECHANICAL ENERGY: The sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy of an object is called its mechanical energy.
Mechanical Energy = KE + PE = (1/2)mv^2 + mgh

EXAMPLES:
(i) Pure Kinetic Energy: A ball rolling on a flat surface (h=0, so PE=0). All mechanical energy is kinetic.
Example: a moving car on a flat road.

(ii) Pure Potential Energy: A ball held stationary at a height (v=0, so KE=0). All mechanical energy is potential.
Example: water stored in a dam reservoir.

(iii) Both KE and PE: A ball rolling down a slope. It has both height (PE) and speed (KE).
Example: a stone thrown at an angle - at any point during flight, it has both height (PE) and velocity (KE).

items.question: A stone is thrown at an angle upward. At the highest point, which statement is CORRECT?

options.B: KE is zero and PE is maximum
options.C: KE is maximum and PE is zero

items.explanation: At the highest point in projectile motion, the vertical component of velocity = 0, but the horizontal component still exists. So KE is NOT zero (horizontal KE remains). PE is maximum. However, if the stone is thrown straight up, KE = 0 and PE = maximum at highest point. The question says 'at an angle' so there is always some horizontal KE. Strictly for straight vertical throw, (B) is correct. For angled throw, (B) is partially correct (PE maximum, KE minimum but not zero).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Objects in motion possess kinetic energy: moving bullet, blowing wind, rotating wheel, speeding stone, flowing water, flying aircraft, running athlete.
Kinetic energy is always positive (both m and v^2 are positive).
KE depends on both mass and velocity, but velocity has more influence (KE proportional to v^2).
If mass doubles: KE doubles.
If velocity doubles: KE becomes 4 times.
Unit of KE is joule (J).
Work-energy theorem: Work done on an object = change in its kinetic energy.
If starting from rest (u=0): W = (1/2)mv^2 = KE.
DERIVATION OF KE FORMULA:
Consider an object of mass m initially at rest (u = 0).
Force F acts on it over displacement s.
Using Newton's 2nd law: F = ma.
Using 3rd equation of motion: v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2as, so a = v^2/(2s).
Work done: W = F x s = ma x s = m x (v^2/2s) x s = (1/2)mv^2.
Since this work is stored as kinetic energy: E_k = W = (1/2)mv^2.

items.question: Define kinetic energy and give two examples of objects possessing kinetic energy.
items.answer:

2. Blowing wind - turns windmill blades because of kinetic energy.
Other examples: flowing water, a rolling ball, a running athlete.

items.question: Derive the SI unit of kinetic energy from its formula E_k = (1/2)mv^2.
items.answer:
E_k = (1/2) x m x v^2
Unit of m = kg
Unit of v = m/s
Unit of v^2 = m^2/s^2
Unit of E_k = kg x m^2/s^2
= kg x m/s^2 x m
= N x m (since N = kg m/s^2)
= joule (J)
Therefore, the SI unit of kinetic energy is joule (J).

items.question: State the work-energy theorem and derive the expression for kinetic energy of an object starting from rest.
items.answer:
WORK-ENERGY THEOREM: The work done on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
W = Delta(KE) = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2

DERIVATION of E_k for object starting from rest (u = 0):
- Let mass = m, initial velocity u = 0, final velocity = v.
- Force F acts through displacement s.
- F = ma (Newton's 2nd law).
- Using v^2 = u^2 + 2as: v^2 = 0 + 2as, so a = v^2/(2s).
- Work done: W = F x s = ma x s = m x (v^2/2s) x s = (1/2)mv^2.
- This work is completely stored as kinetic energy.
- Therefore: E_k = (1/2)mv^2.

items.question: A car of mass 1500 kg is moving with velocity 30 km/h. Find its kinetic energy. What would be its kinetic energy if velocity is doubled to 60 km/h?
items.answer:
GIVEN:
m = 1500 kg
v1 = 30 km/h = 30 x (1000/3600) = 8.33 m/s (approx) = 25/3 m/s
v2 = 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s

KINETIC ENERGY AT 30 km/h:
E_k1 = (1/2) x 1500 x (25/3)^2
= (1/2) x 1500 x 625/9
= (750 x 625)/9
= 468750/9
= 52083.33 J approx 52083 J

KINETIC ENERGY AT 60 km/h:
E_k2 = (1/2) x 1500 x (50/3)^2
= (1/2) x 1500 x 2500/9
= (750 x 2500)/9
= 1875000/9
= 208333.33 J approx 208333 J

RATIO: E_k2/E_k1 = 208333/52083 = 4.
When velocity is doubled, kinetic energy becomes 4 times. This confirms E_k proportional to v^2.

items.question: An object of mass m moving with velocity of 5 m/s has kinetic energy of 25 J. What will be its kinetic energy when its velocity is doubled? What will be the velocity?
items.answer:
GIVEN:
E_k1 = 25 J when v1 = 5 m/s
Find mass m:
E_k1 = (1/2)mv1^2
25 = (1/2) x m x 25
m = 25 x 2/25 = 2 kg

WHEN VELOCITY IS DOUBLED (v2 = 10 m/s):
E_k2 = (1/2) x 2 x (10)^2
= (1/2) x 2 x 100
= 100 J

ALTERNATIVELY: Since E_k is proportional to v^2:
E_k2/E_k1 = (v2/v1)^2 = (10/5)^2 = 4
E_k2 = 4 x E_k1 = 4 x 25 = 100 J.

WHEN VELOCITY IS TRIPLED (v3 = 15 m/s):
E_k3 = (1/2) x 2 x (15)^2 = 1 x 225 = 225 J.
Or: E_k3 = 9 x 25 = 225 J (since 3^2 = 9).

items.question: A bullet of mass 10 g is fired from a gun with a muzzle velocity of 400 m/s. (i) Find the kinetic energy of the bullet. (ii) Find the work done by the gun on the bullet. (iii) If the bullet embeds in a target and comes to rest, what happens to its kinetic energy? (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
GIVEN:
Mass of bullet, m = 10 g = 10/1000 = 0.01 kg
Initial velocity (at rest in gun), u = 0 m/s
Muzzle velocity, v = 400 m/s

(i) KINETIC ENERGY OF BULLET:
E_k = (1/2)mv^2
= (1/2) x 0.01 x (400)^2
= (1/2) x 0.01 x 160000
= 0.01 x 80000
= 800 J
Kinetic energy of the bullet = 800 J.

(ii) WORK DONE BY GUN ON BULLET:
By work-energy theorem:
Work done = Change in KE = Final KE - Initial KE
= (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2
= 800 J - 0
= 800 J
Work done by the gun on the bullet = 800 J.
(Chemical energy of gunpowder is converted to kinetic energy of bullet.)

(iii) WHAT HAPPENS WHEN BULLET STOPS IN TARGET:
When bullet embeds in target and comes to rest:
Final KE = 0.
Initial KE = 800 J.
By law of conservation of energy, the 800 J is converted to:
- Heat energy (bullet and target get hot due to friction).
- Sound energy (bang when bullet hits target).
- Deformation energy (target gets deformed/damaged).
Total energy is conserved - 800 J is distributed as heat, sound and deformation energy.

items.question: Define potential energy and give two examples from daily life.
items.answer:
DEFINITION: Potential energy is the energy possessed by an object by virtue of its position or its configuration (shape/deformation).
Formula (gravitational): E_p = mgh.

Examples:
1. Water stored in a dam at a height - possesses gravitational PE.
2. A stretched rubber band - possesses elastic PE due to deformation.
Other examples: wound clock spring, a raised hammer, a drawn bow.

items.question: With the help of Activities 10.8 and 10.9, explain how potential energy is stored in a rubber band and a slinky.
items.answer:
RUBBER BAND (Activity 10.8):
- When rubber band is stretched, work is done on it (force x extension).
- This work is stored as elastic potential energy in the deformed rubber band.
- When released, elastic PE converts to kinetic energy (band snaps back).
- More stretch = more elastic PE stored.

SLINKY (Activity 10.9):
- When slinky is stretched by pulling its ends apart, work is done against the elastic restoring force.
- This work is stored as elastic potential energy.
- When released, elastic PE converts to kinetic energy (slinky contracts).
- The energy was transferred TO the spring when stretched, and FROM the spring when released.

KEY POINT: In both cases, energy input (work done on object) = energy stored (as PE) = energy output (as KE when released). This illustrates energy storage and the conservation principle.

items.question: A bow and arrow system demonstrates potential energy. Explain the energy transformations when (i) the bow is drawn, (ii) the arrow is released, and (iii) the arrow hits a target.
items.answer:
(i) BOW IS DRAWN:
- Archer does work by pulling the bowstring (force x displacement).
- This work is stored as elastic potential energy in the bent bow and stretched string.
- The more the bow is drawn, the more elastic PE is stored.
- Kinetic energy = 0 (bow is stationary when fully drawn).
- Energy: W = stored PE.

(ii) ARROW IS RELEASED:
- Elastic PE of bow converts to kinetic energy of arrow.
- PE of bow decreases as it returns to original shape.
- Arrow accelerates from rest and gains KE.
- Total energy: PE of bow = KE of arrow + heat (small, due to air resistance and string vibration).
- Energy transformation: Elastic PE -> KE.

(iii) ARROW HITS TARGET:
- KE of moving arrow is used to do work on target (penetrate or push it).
- Arrow slows down (KE decreases).
- Target material gets pushed/deformed.
- KE converts to: deformation energy of target + heat (due to friction) + sound.
- Total energy is conserved throughout.

items.question: Define gravitational potential energy and write its formula with explanation.
items.answer:
DEFINITION: Gravitational potential energy is the energy stored in an object due to its position above the ground (or any reference level). It is equal to the work done against gravity in raising the object to that height.

Formula: E_p = mgh
Where:
m = mass of the object (in kg)
g = acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/s^2 or 10 m/s^2 approx)
h = height above reference level (in m)
E_p = gravitational potential energy (in joules, J).

items.question: An object of mass 5 kg is raised to a height of 3 m. Calculate its potential energy. (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given:
m = 5 kg, h = 3 m, g = 10 m/s^2.
E_p = mgh
= 5 x 10 x 3
= 150 J.
The potential energy of the object is 150 J.
(This equals the work done in lifting it: W = F x s = mg x h = 5 x 10 x 3 = 150 J.)

items.question: Derive the expression for gravitational potential energy of an object of mass m at height h.
items.answer:
DERIVATION:
Consider an object of mass m lying at rest on the ground (reference level, h = 0).

Step 1: To lift the object, we apply an upward force just equal to its weight (minimum force needed).
Upward force F = mg (weight of object).

Step 2: Object is raised through vertical height h (from ground to height h).
Displacement = h (in direction of applied force).

Step 3: Work done by the applied force:
W = Force x Displacement = F x h = mg x h = mgh.

Step 4: This work done against gravity is stored as potential energy in the object.
E_p = W = mgh.

Therefore, E_p = mgh.
Note: This energy is released when the object falls back to the ground level.

items.question: A stone of mass 2 kg is dropped from a building. Just before it hits the ground, its velocity is 20 m/s. From what height was it dropped? Also find its initial PE. (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given: m = 2 kg, u = 0 (dropped), v = 20 m/s just before hitting ground.

STEP 1 - FIND HEIGHT:
Using v^2 = u^2 + 2gh (taking downward as positive):
(20)^2 = 0 + 2 x 10 x h
400 = 20h
h = 20 m.
The stone was dropped from 20 m height.

STEP 2 - FIND INITIAL PE:
E_p = mgh = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 J.

VERIFICATION (using KE at ground):
KE at ground = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2) x 2 x (20)^2 = (1/2) x 2 x 400 = 400 J.
Initial PE (400 J) = Final KE (400 J). Energy is conserved.

items.question: An object of mass 12 kg is at a certain height. Its potential energy is 480 J. Find the height. If the object is dropped from this height, find its velocity just before hitting the ground. (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
PART A - FIND HEIGHT:
E_p = mgh
480 = 12 x 10 x h
480 = 120h
h = 480/120 = 4 m.
The object is at a height of 4 m.

PART B - VELOCITY ON REACHING GROUND:
Using conservation of energy:
Initial PE = Final KE (at ground)
mgh = (1/2)mv^2
gh = (1/2)v^2
v^2 = 2gh = 2 x 10 x 4 = 80
v = sqrt(80) = 4sqrt(5) approx 8.94 m/s.

Alternatively: v^2 = u^2 + 2gh = 0 + 2 x 10 x 4 = 80
v = sqrt(80) = approx 8.94 m/s.
Velocity just before hitting ground = approx 8.94 m/s.

items.question: Activity 10.15 type: An object of mass 20 kg is dropped from a height of 4 m. Complete the table showing PE, KE and total energy at heights 4 m, 3 m, 2 m, 1 m and just above ground. (Take g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given: m = 20 kg, initial height h = 4 m, g = 10 m/s^2.
Total mechanical energy = Initial PE = mgh = 20 x 10 x 4 = 800 J (constant throughout).

AT HEIGHT 4 m (just released):
PE = mgh = 20 x 10 x 4 = 800 J
KE = 0 (starts from rest)
Total = 800 J

AT HEIGHT 3 m (fallen 1 m):
PE = 20 x 10 x 3 = 600 J
KE = 800 - 600 = 200 J
(Check: v^2 = 2g(1) = 20, KE = (1/2)(20)(20) = 200 J.) Correct.
Total = 800 J

AT HEIGHT 2 m (fallen 2 m):
PE = 20 x 10 x 2 = 400 J
KE = 800 - 400 = 400 J
Total = 800 J

AT HEIGHT 1 m (fallen 3 m):
PE = 20 x 10 x 1 = 200 J
KE = 800 - 200 = 600 J
Total = 800 J

JUST ABOVE GROUND (height = 0, fallen 4 m):
PE = 0 J
KE = 800 J
(Check: v^2 = 2g x 4 = 80, KE = (1/2)(20)(80) = 800 J.) Correct.
Total = 800 J

CONCLUSION: At every height, PE + KE = 800 J = constant. As object falls, PE decreases and KE increases by equal amounts. Total mechanical energy is conserved.

items.question: Gravitational potential energy of an object depends on:

options.D: the path taken to reach that height

items.explanation: E_p = mgh. PE depends on mass (m), gravitational acceleration (g) and height (h) above reference level. It does NOT depend on velocity or path taken to reach that height.

items.question: If height of an object is doubled, its gravitational PE becomes:
items.explanation: E_p = mgh. If h becomes 2h: E_p_new = mg(2h) = 2mgh = 2E_p. PE is directly proportional to height.

items.question: A 5 kg object is at height 10 m. Its PE (g = 10 m/s^2) and its velocity when it reaches the ground are:
Why is gravitational PE said to be independent of path taken to reach a height?

options.B: Gravity is a conservative force that acts only vertically

items.explanation: Gravity acts only in the vertical direction. Horizontal motion requires no work against gravity. Therefore, only vertical height matters, not the path. This path-independence is the defining property of conservative forces like gravity.

items.question: A ball of mass 2 kg is thrown upward with KE = 200 J. How high will it rise? (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.explanation: At maximum height, all KE converts to PE: KE = PE. 200 = mgh = 2 x 10 x h = 20h. h = 200/20 = 10 m. Conservation of energy: initial KE = final PE (at max height where v = 0).

items.question: Give two examples of energy conversion from nature and two from human-made devices.
items.answer:
FROM NATURE:
1. Photosynthesis: Green plants convert solar (light) energy into chemical energy stored in food (glucose).
2. Waterfall: Water at height (gravitational PE) converts to KE as it falls.

FROM HUMAN-MADE DEVICES:
1. Electric bulb: Electrical energy converts to light energy and heat energy.
2. Battery: Chemical energy converts to electrical energy.

items.question: Describe the energy conversions involved when coal is burned to drive a steam engine.
items.answer:
STEP-BY-STEP ENERGY CONVERSIONS:

Step 1: Coal burns (Chemical energy -> Heat energy).
Chemical energy stored in coal (from ancient plant matter) is released as heat when coal burns in the furnace.

Step 2: Heat boils water (Heat energy -> Heat energy of steam under pressure).
The heat converts water to steam. Steam under high pressure has both thermal energy and pressure potential energy.

Step 3: Steam drives pistons (Thermal/Pressure energy -> Kinetic energy).
High pressure steam pushes pistons, converting steam energy to kinetic energy of moving pistons.

Step 4: Pistons turn wheels (Kinetic energy -> Kinetic energy of wheels).
The reciprocating motion of pistons is converted to rotational kinetic energy of the engine wheels.

Overall transformation: Chemical energy (coal) -> Kinetic energy (wheels).
At each step, some energy is lost as heat to the surroundings, but total energy is conserved.

items.question: During photosynthesis, solar energy is converted to chemical energy. Where is this chemical energy ultimately stored?

options.A: In the roots of the plant

items.explanation: Photosynthesis converts light energy + CO2 + H2O into glucose (C6H12O6) + O2. The chemical energy is stored in the bonds of glucose molecules - the food of the plant.

items.question: A battery-operated toy car converts energy in what sequence?
items.explanation: Battery stores chemical energy -> chemical energy converts to electrical energy as battery discharges -> electrical energy powers motor -> motor converts electrical energy to kinetic energy (motion of car).

items.question: Coal and petroleum are called 'stored solar energy'. Explain why this statement is scientifically correct in terms of energy transformation.

options.A: Because coal and petroleum come from the sun
options.B: Because ancient plants stored solar energy as chemical energy, which was preserved in coal/petroleum
options.D: Because coal is made of sunlight

items.explanation: Millions of years ago, living plants and organisms captured solar energy through photosynthesis and stored it as chemical energy. When they died, they decomposed under pressure and heat to form coal and petroleum. So these fuels contain ancient solar energy in chemical form - hence they are 'stored solar energy'. When burned, this chemical energy is released as heat.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Total mechanical energy = KE + PE = constant (for objects with no friction/air resistance).
For a freely falling object: at any point, mgh + (1/2)mv^2 = constant = initial PE.
At height h: KE = 0, PE = mgh, total = mgh.
At height h/2: KE = mgh/2, PE = mgh/2, total = mgh.
At ground: KE = mgh, PE = 0, total = mgh.
This law applies to all forms of energy (not just mechanical).
Energy appears to be 'lost' in practice due to conversion to heat (friction, air resistance) - but total energy including heat is still conserved.
The law was verified experimentally by James Prescott Joule.
MATHEMATICAL PROOF (Free Fall):
Object of mass m falls from height h (starting from rest).
At any intermediate height x (measured from ground):
Velocity v^2 = 2g(h-x) (using v^2 = u^2 + 2as, with a = g, s = h-x)
PE = mgx
Total = KE + PE = mg(h-x) + mgx = mgh - mgx + mgx = mgh = constant.
Therefore, total mechanical energy is constant at every point during free fall.

items.question: State the law of conservation of energy.
items.answer:
The law of conservation of energy states that: Energy can only be converted from one form to another; it can neither be created nor destroyed.
Equivalently: The total energy of a system before and after any energy transformation always remains the same.
This law is valid in all situations and for all kinds of energy transformations.

items.question: For a freely falling object, show that the sum of KE and PE remains constant at any point during the fall.
items.answer:
Consider object of mass m at any intermediate height x from the ground during free fall from height h.
- Velocity at this point: v^2 = 2g(h-x) (from equations of motion)
- KE = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2)m x 2g(h-x) = mg(h-x)
- PE = mgx
- Total mechanical energy = KE + PE = mg(h-x) + mgx = mgh - mgx + mgx = mgh.

Since mgh is a constant (m, g, h are all fixed), the total mechanical energy is constant at every point during free fall.

items.question: A pendulum bob swings from one extreme to another. Explain the energy transformation and show that total mechanical energy is conserved.
items.answer:
Consider pendulum bob swinging from extreme A to lowest point O to extreme B.

AT EXTREME A (highest point):
- Velocity = 0 (momentarily at rest).
- KE = 0.
- PE = mgh (where h = height of A above O).
- Total = mgh.

AT LOWEST POINT O:
- Velocity is maximum (v_max).
- PE = 0 (reference level).
- KE = (1/2)mv_max^2.
- By conservation of energy: (1/2)mv_max^2 = mgh, so v_max = sqrt(2gh).
- Total = mgh.

AT EXTREME B (same height h as A):
- Velocity = 0 (momentarily at rest again).
- KE = 0.
- PE = mgh.
- Total = mgh.

CONCLUSION: At every point, Total = mgh = constant. PE continuously converts to KE and back to PE. This demonstrates conservation of mechanical energy.

(In reality, pendulum gradually slows due to air resistance - mechanical energy converts to heat. But total energy including heat is still conserved.)

items.question: An object of mass 2 kg is thrown upward with velocity 20 m/s. (i) Find its KE at the moment of throwing. (ii) Find its maximum height. (iii) Find its PE at maximum height. (iv) Verify conservation of energy.
items.answer:
Given: m = 2 kg, u = 20 m/s, g = 10 m/s^2.

(i) KE AT THROWING:
E_k = (1/2)mu^2 = (1/2) x 2 x (20)^2 = 1 x 400 = 400 J.

(ii) MAXIMUM HEIGHT:
At maximum height, v = 0. Using v^2 = u^2 - 2gh (retardation due to gravity):
0 = (20)^2 - 2 x 10 x h
20h = 400
h = 20 m.

(iii) PE AT MAXIMUM HEIGHT:
E_p = mgh = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 J.

(iv) VERIFICATION:
Initial state: KE = 400 J, PE = 0 (ground level), Total = 400 J.
At maximum height: KE = 0, PE = 400 J, Total = 400 J.
Both totals are equal. Conservation of energy is verified.
Initial KE = Final PE (400 J). Energy converted from KE to PE completely. No energy gained or lost.

items.question: A rock of mass 5 kg is at the top of a cliff 20 m high. (i) Find its PE. (ii) Find its velocity just before hitting the base of cliff. (iii) Find its KE just before hitting. (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given: m = 5 kg, h = 20 m, g = 10 m/s^2.

(i) PE AT TOP OF CLIFF:
E_p = mgh = 5 x 10 x 20 = 1000 J.

(ii) VELOCITY JUST BEFORE HITTING GROUND:
Using conservation of energy (PE at top = KE at bottom):
mgh = (1/2)mv^2
v^2 = 2gh = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400
v = sqrt(400) = 20 m/s.

Alternatively: v^2 = u^2 + 2gh = 0 + 2 x 10 x 20 = 400. v = 20 m/s.

(iii) KE JUST BEFORE HITTING:
E_k = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2) x 5 x (20)^2 = (1/2) x 5 x 400 = 1000 J.

Note: Initial PE (1000 J) = Final KE (1000 J). Energy is conserved.

items.question: Explain with detailed steps how the law of conservation of energy is demonstrated in a freely falling stone of mass 3 kg dropped from 5 m height. Calculate PE, KE and total energy at heights 5 m, 2.5 m and 0 m. (g = 10 m/s^2)
items.answer:
Given: m = 3 kg, h = 5 m, g = 10 m/s^2.
Total mechanical energy = Initial PE = mgh = 3 x 10 x 5 = 150 J (this must remain constant).

AT HEIGHT 5 m (starting point, u = 0):
PE = mgh = 3 x 10 x 5 = 150 J
KE = (1/2)mu^2 = 0 (at rest)
Total energy = 150 + 0 = 150 J

AT HEIGHT 2.5 m (midway, fallen 2.5 m):
Distance fallen = 5 - 2.5 = 2.5 m
v^2 = 2 x g x distance fallen = 2 x 10 x 2.5 = 50
KE = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2) x 3 x 50 = 75 J
PE = mgh = 3 x 10 x 2.5 = 75 J
Total energy = 75 + 75 = 150 J

AT HEIGHT 0 m (ground level, fallen 5 m):
v^2 = 2 x g x 5 = 100
KE = (1/2)mv^2 = (1/2) x 3 x 100 = 150 J
PE = mgh = 3 x 10 x 0 = 0 J
Total energy = 150 + 0 = 150 J

sections.label: SUMMARY TABLE:
sections.text:
Height | PE   | KE   | Total
5 m    | 150 J| 0 J  | 150 J
2.5 m  | 75 J | 75 J | 150 J
0 m    | 0 J  | 150 J| 150 J

CONCLUSION: At every height during free fall, the total mechanical energy = 150 J = constant.
- PE decreases as stone falls (height decreases).
- KE increases as stone falls (velocity increases).
- Decrease in PE = Increase in KE at every point.
- Total energy is conserved. This verifies the law of conservation of energy.

items.explanation: For free fall (no friction/air resistance), total mechanical energy = KE + PE = constant throughout. As height decreases (PE decreases), velocity increases (KE increases) by equal amounts.

items.question: An object hits the ground after falling. Where does its kinetic energy go?

options.B: It converts to heat, sound and deformation of ground
options.C: It converts back to potential energy

items.explanation: By law of conservation of energy, energy cannot be destroyed. When object hits ground, KE converts to heat (due to impact friction), sound (impact sound) and deformation energy (ground gets dented). Total energy is conserved.

items.question: A pendulum clock eventually stops. This is because:

options.A: law of conservation of energy is violated
options.B: energy is destroyed by the pendulum
options.C: KE and PE convert to heat due to air resistance and friction
options.D: the clock uses up energy and creates none

items.explanation: The pendulum loses a small amount of mechanical energy at each swing due to air resistance and friction at the pivot. This mechanical energy converts to heat (not destroyed). Eventually all mechanical energy is converted to heat and pendulum stops. Total energy (mechanical + heat) remains conserved. Clock batteries/springs replace this lost energy in running clocks.

items.question: An object of mass 1 kg is thrown up with velocity 10 m/s. Its total mechanical energy throughout flight (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
items.explanation: Total mechanical energy = initial KE (at ground, PE = 0) = (1/2)(1)(10)^2 = 50 J. By conservation of energy, this remains 50 J throughout (ignoring air resistance). At max height: PE = 50 J, KE = 0 J, total = 50 J.

items.question: A ball falls from 10 m, bounces off the floor and rises to 8 m. The percentage of energy lost in the bounce is:
items.explanation: Initial PE = mgh = mg x 10. After bounce, PE = mg x 8. Energy lost = mg x 10 - mg x 8 = mg x 2. Percentage lost = (2/10) x 100 = 20%. The energy 'lost' actually converts to heat and sound during the bounce. 20% of mechanical energy is converted to heat and sound.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Power = Work done / Time taken: P = W/t.
SI unit of power: watt (W). 1 W = 1 J s^-1.
Larger unit: kilowatt (kW). 1 kW = 1000 W = 1000 J s^-1.
Average power: Total energy consumed / Total time taken.
A stronger/more powerful agent does the same work in less time.
Power describes how fast or slow work is done.
Commercial unit of electrical energy: kilowatt hour (kWh). 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 3600000 J.
1 watt = 1 joule/second.
Power can also be written as: P = (F x s)/t = F x v (where v = s/t = velocity).
Power measures the speed of energy transfer, not the total amount.
CONVERSIONS:
DO YOU KNOW: James Watt (1736-1819) developed the modern steam engine. The unit watt is named after him.
EXAMPLE 10.7 (Textbook):
Two girls, each of weight 400 N, climb a rope 8 m high. Girl A takes 20 s, Girl B takes 50 s. Find power expended by each.
For B: Power = 3200/50 = 64 W.
A expends more power - she does the same work in less time.
EXAMPLE 10.8 (Textbook):
Boy of mass 50 kg runs up staircase of 45 steps, each 15 cm high, in 9 s. (g = 10 m/s^2)

items.question: Define power and write its SI unit and formula.
items.answer:
DEFINITION: Power is the rate of doing work, or equivalently, the rate of transfer of energy.
FORMULA: P = W/t
Where P = power, W = work done (in J), t = time taken (in s).
SI UNIT: Watt (W). 1 W = 1 J/s.
Larger unit: Kilowatt (kW). 1 kW = 1000 W.

items.question: Define 1 watt of power.
items.answer:
1 watt is defined as the power of an agent that does work at the rate of 1 joule per second.
1 W = 1 J s^-1 = 1 J/s.
We can also say power is 1 W when the rate of consumption of energy is 1 J per second.

items.question: What is 1 kilowatt hour (kWh)? How many joules equal 1 kWh?
items.answer:
1 kilowatt hour (kWh) is the commercial unit of electrical energy. It is the energy consumed when a device of power 1 kilowatt works for 1 hour.
1 kWh = 1 kW x 1 hour = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
Note: 1 kWh = 1 'unit' of electricity as used in electricity bills.

items.question: A lamp consumes 1000 J of electrical energy in 10 seconds. What is its power?
items.answer:
Given: W = 1000 J, t = 10 s.
Power P = W/t = 1000/10 = 100 J/s = 100 W.
The power of the lamp is 100 watts.

items.question: What is the unit of power named after and why?
items.answer: The SI unit of power is named watt (W) after James Watt (1736-1819), a Scottish inventor and mechanical engineer. He developed the modern steam engine and made significant contributions to the Industrial Revolution. The unit was named in his honour because of his work on studying and improving the concept of power in machines.

items.question: A household has consumed 250 units (kWh) of energy during a month. How much energy is this in joules?
items.answer:
250 units = 250 kWh.
1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
250 kWh = 250 x 3.6 x 10^6 J = 900 x 10^6 J = 9 x 10^8 J.
The energy consumed = 9 x 10^8 joules.

items.question: Two girls, A and B, each of weight 400 N, climb a rope 8 m high. A takes 20 s and B takes 50 s. Who does more work? Who has more power? Explain.
items.answer:
WORK DONE BY EACH:
Work = Force x Displacement = Weight x Height = 400 x 8 = 3200 J.
Both A and B do the same work (3200 J), because work depends on force and displacement, not time.

POWER OF A:
P_A = W/t = 3200/20 = 160 W.

POWER OF B:
P_B = W/t = 3200/50 = 64 W.

A has more power (160 W > 64 W). Although both do the same total work, A does it faster (in less time), so A's rate of doing work is higher. Power measures how fast work is done, not the total amount.

items.question: Explain with an example the difference between work done and power.
items.answer:
WORK DONE: Work = Force x Displacement. It measures the total energy transferred. It does NOT depend on time.

POWER: Power = Work/Time. It measures the rate of energy transfer. It DOES depend on time.

EXAMPLE: Two engines, A and B, both do 10,000 J of work in moving a train.
- Engine A takes 10 seconds: P_A = 10000/10 = 1000 W.
- Engine B takes 100 seconds: P_B = 10000/100 = 100 W.

Both engines do the same work (10,000 J). But Engine A is 10 times more powerful because it does the work 10 times faster. Power tells us about the efficiency (speed) of doing work, while work done tells us about the total energy transferred.

items.question: A certain household consumes 250 units of electricity in a month. What does this mean? Calculate the cost at 5 rupees per unit.
items.answer:
250 UNITS MEANS:
1 unit of electricity = 1 kWh (kilowatt hour).
250 units = 250 kWh = energy consumed when 1000 W appliances run for 250 hours, or 100 W appliances run for 2500 hours.
In joules: 250 kWh = 250 x 3.6 x 10^6 = 9 x 10^8 J = 900 million joules.

COST CALCULATION:
Cost per unit = Rs. 5.
Total cost = 250 units x Rs. 5 per unit = Rs. 1250.

The household must pay Rs. 1250 for the month's electricity.

This shows why using high-power appliances for many hours makes electricity bills expensive. Conservation of electricity means using less energy over time.

items.question: A boy of mass 50 kg runs up a staircase of 45 steps in 9 s. If the height of each step is 15 cm, calculate his power. (g = 10 m/s^2)

items.question: Find the energy in joules consumed in 10 hours by four devices each of power 500 W. Also find the cost at Rs. 3 per unit.
items.answer:
Given:
Number of devices = 4, power of each = 500 W.
Time = 10 hours.

TOTAL POWER: 4 x 500 = 2000 W = 2 kW.

ENERGY CONSUMED:
Energy = Power x Time = 2 kW x 10 h = 20 kWh = 20 units.

IN JOULES:
20 kWh = 20 x 3.6 x 10^6 J = 72 x 10^6 J = 7.2 x 10^7 J.

COST:
Total cost = 20 units x Rs. 3 per unit = Rs. 60.

The energy consumed is 7.2 x 10^7 joules and the cost is Rs. 60.

items.question: Power is defined as:
items.explanation: Power = Work done / Time taken = Rate of doing work. P = W/t. It measures how quickly work is done or how fast energy is transferred.

items.question: The SI unit of power is:
items.explanation: The SI unit of power is watt (W), named after James Watt. 1 W = 1 J/s. Joule is unit of energy, newton is unit of force, pascal is unit of pressure.

items.question: 1 watt equals:
items.explanation: 1 W = 1 joule per second = 1 J/s. Power is the rate of doing work, so it equals work divided by time.

items.question: 1 kilowatt (kW) equals:
items.explanation: Kilo means 1000. So 1 kW = 1000 W. This is used for larger power values like electric motors, engines, etc.

items.question: A device uses 600 J of energy in 2 minutes. Its power is:
items.explanation: t = 2 min = 120 s. P = W/t = 600/120 = 5 W. Always convert time to seconds before calculating power.

items.question: Two workers A and B do the same 1000 J of work. A takes 10 s and B takes 20 s. What is true?

options.A: A is more powerful than B
options.B: B is more powerful than A

items.explanation: P_A = 1000/10 = 100 W. P_B = 1000/20 = 50 W. A is more powerful because he does the same work in less time. Power = Work/Time, so less time = more power for same work.

items.question: A 100 W bulb works for 2 hours. Energy consumed in kWh is:
items.explanation: Energy = Power x Time = 100 W x 2 h = 100 W x 2 h = 0.1 kW x 2 h = 0.2 kWh. The bulb uses 0.2 units of electricity. (Or: 100 W x 2 x 3600 s = 720000 J = 0.2 kWh).

items.question: Power can also be expressed as:
items.explanation: P = W/t = (F x s)/t = F x (s/t) = F x v. So power = force x velocity. This is useful when calculating power of engines or motors moving at constant velocity.

items.question: The commercial unit of electricity is:
items.explanation: The commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt hour (kWh), also called a 'unit'. Electricity bills are calculated in kWh. 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

items.question: A pump can lift 500 kg of water through 3 m in 10 s. (g = 10 m/s^2). Power of pump is:
items.explanation: Work done = mgh = 500 x 10 x 3 = 15000 J. Time = 10 s. Power = W/t = 15000/10 = 1500 W = 1.5 kW.

items.question: A machine does 36000 J of work in 1 hour. Its power in watts is:
items.explanation: t = 1 hour = 3600 s. P = W/t = 36000/3600 = 10 W. The machine has very low power of 10 W despite doing 36000 J of work (because it takes a long time - 1 hour).

items.question: An electric motor rated 1.5 kW powers a machine for 3 hours. Energy consumed in joules is:
items.explanation: Energy = Power x Time = 1.5 kW x 3 h = 4.5 kWh. Converting: 4.5 kWh = 4.5 x 3.6 x 10^6 J = 16.2 x 10^6 J = 1.62 x 10^7 J. Always convert to SI: 1500 W x (3 x 3600 s) = 1500 x 10800 = 16,200,000 J = 1.62 x 10^7 J.
